nodes.title: Levers and Pulleys
segments: People have always looked for ways to move heavy things with less effort. The oldest answers are also the simplest ones: a rigid bar, a rope and a wheel. This chapter looks at two of them.

nodes.title: 1.1 Levers
segments: A lever is a rigid bar that turns around a fixed point called the fulcrum. When the fulcrum sits close to the load, a small push on the far end lifts a large weight. The hand moves a long way while the load moves a short way, and the computation behind it is simple enough to do in your head.

Seesaws, crowbars and bottle openers are all levers. A seesaw puts the fulcrum in the middle, so two children of similar weight can balance each other when they sit at equal distances from the middle of the board.
A crowbar works the other way round: the fulcrum sits near the heavy end, and a long handle turns a modest push into a strong lift.[^1] Builders relied on this long before anyone wrote the rule down.
Three things decide how well a lever works:
how long each arm is; and
how stiff the bar stays under load, which matters most when the load is heavy and the bar is thin.
A famous boast claims that a long enough lever could move the whole Earth.

nodes.title: 1.2 Pulleys
segments: A pulley is a wheel with a groove for a rope. One fixed pulley only changes the direction of the pull, but several pulleys working together share the load between many lengths of rope.
Figure 1.1 — A block and tackle with four supporting ropes.

nodes.title: Gears
segments: A gear is a wheel with teeth. When two gears mesh, the smaller one turns faster and the larger one turns with more force, a trade that engineers call *mechanical advantage*.
Modern self-driving carts still depend on gear trains hidden inside their wheels.
Even the small self-driving carts in a warehouse count on gears to turn quick motor spins into slow, strong wheel turns.
